newsitem.title: USA: UPS, striking Teamsters set to resume talks.
newsitem.headline: UPS, striking Teamsters set to resume talks.

text.p: The Teamsters Union and United Parcel Service were to head back to the bargaining table on Thursday, but with few hopes of ending the strike that has crippled the nation's largest package delivery company.

The only thing the two sides seemed to agree on ahead of the 2 p.m. EDT (1800 GMT) meeting was that there was little room to negotiate. With the strike in its fourth day, the parties face unresolved issues, including pay and benefits, the company's use of part-time workers and pensions.
UPS -- which normally handles 12 million packages a day -- reiterated that it was unwilling to make any significant changes to its last offer, made before the strike began.
"UPS remains committed to its final contract offer and is encouraging the union leaders to let UPS Teamsters vote on the proposal," the company said in a statement.
Teamster President Ron Carey said that if UPS was unwilling to negotiate big changes to its offer, there could be no contract.
"We have seen no sign that the company has changed its attitude, so we are not particularly optimistic about these new talks," Carey said late on Wednesday.
Carey will meet with UPS negotiator Dave Murray with the help of a federal mediator, John Calhoun Wells.
The announcement on Wednesday that talks would resume was welcomed by businesses, which have faced headaches getting packages delivered and higher shipping costs from overloaded UPS rivals.

The strike by 185,000 Teamsters began at a minute past midnight EDT on Monday (0401 GMT) after a last-ditch effort to avoid a work stoppage collapsed. The two sides sat through 17 hours of talks with a mediator but wound up deadlocked.

The Teamsters blamed the strike on the company's refusal to create thousands of full-time jobs each year from part-time positions and to stop handing union work to outside suppliers. Part-timers account for 60 percent of the 301,000 domestic workers at Atlanta-based UPS.

UPS called those issues "a smoke screen," saying the real issue was the Teamsters' refusal to let the company withdraw from a multi-employer pension plan that includes 30 other companies, mostly trucking firms.

Since the strike began, UPS has been handling less than 10 percent of its normal shipments, using 50,000 non-union employees to do the work of striking loaders, sorters and drivers. The company also said that more than 5,000 Teamster members were reporting to work, crossing union picket lines.
The two sides agreed to meet after days of pressure from the Clinton administration, though the White House has resisted calls to step in and end the strike.
Business leaders warned that there would be massive layoffs at small- and mid-size firms struggling to move their goods if the strikers were not ordered back to work.

But Clinton told a White House news conference on Wednesday he could only intervene by invoking the Taft-Hartley Law, which authorises the president to halt strikes that threaten the nation's safety or economic health.
"There has to be a severe damage to the country. The test is ... very high before the president can intervene," he said.
